source_note: Compiled from the cognitive-bias literature as documented in peer-reviewed sources and the Wikipedia 'List of cognitive biases' (curated, deduplicated), supplemented by entries on collective-deliberation and informational-environment failure modes drawn from the political-science, organizational-behavior, and information-environment literatures. Each entry carries an operational definition and a 'government_decision_cue' string — the detection signal the classifier agent looks for in the record. The 'layer' field maps each entry to METHODOLOGY.md §5/§5a: 'L1' = individual cognitive bias, 'L2' = group dynamic, 'L3' = informational closure / echo chamber.

categories.decision_and_belief: Biases affecting how evidence is weighed and conclusions formed.
categories.social: Biases driven by relation to other people or groups.
categories.memory: Biases in recall and reconstruction of events.
categories.probability_and_risk: Biases in estimating likelihoods, frequencies, and risks.
categories.framing_and_anchoring: Biases driven by how options or numbers are presented.
categories.self_assessment: Biases about one's own abilities, knowledge, or agency.
categories.motivation_and_identity: Biases arising from what the decider wants to be true.
categories.group: Failure modes that emerge in collective deliberation. L2 layer (see METHODOLOGY.md §5a).
categories.attribution: Biases in assigning causes to behaviors and outcomes.
categories.informational_environment: Structural conditions of the information environment the deliberating body operated inside — source diet, briefing pipeline, advisor composition, exposure to contradiction. L3 layer (see METHODOLOGY.md §5a). These are properties of the room, not of the people inside it.

biases.name: Confirmation bias
biases.definition: Tendency to search for, interpret, and recall information that confirms one's prior beliefs.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy rationale cites only supporting studies; contrary evidence in the record is acknowledged only to dismiss it or is absent entirely.

biases.name: Anchoring
biases.definition: Over-reliance on the first piece of numerical information encountered when making subsequent estimates.
biases.government_decision_cue: A budget, target, or threshold matches a prior round's number with no stated reason, or the first figure floated by a senior official becomes the final figure with no analytic re-derivation.

biases.name: Availability heuristic
biases.definition: Judging the probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind.
biases.government_decision_cue: Risk assessment overweights recent or mediagenic events while treating common-but-quiet risks as background noise.

biases.name: Representativeness heuristic
biases.definition: Judging probability by how much an outcome resembles a mental prototype, neglecting base rates.
biases.government_decision_cue: A case is treated as typical of a category based on surface features, ignoring the prevalence of that category in the relevant population.

biases.name: Base-rate neglect
biases.definition: Ignoring general statistical information in favor of case-specific information.
biases.government_decision_cue: Decision cites a vivid individual case or anecdote without reference to the underlying population statistics the policy will actually operate on.

biases.name: Dunning–Kruger effect
biases.definition: People with low ability in a domain overestimate their competence in that domain.
biases.government_decision_cue: An official without documented domain expertise makes categorical technical claims and overrides published expert advice.

biases.name: Overconfidence effect
biases.definition: Subjective confidence in one's judgments is reliably greater than objective accuracy.
biases.government_decision_cue: Projections are stated without confidence intervals, or the bands given are far narrower than the class of forecast historically supports.

biases.name: Planning fallacy
biases.definition: Systematic underestimation of the time, cost, and risk of future actions.
biases.government_decision_cue: Public timelines and cost estimates match best-case internal numbers without adjustment for the reference class of similar public projects.

biases.name: Optimism bias
biases.definition: Tendency to believe one is less likely than others to experience a negative event.
biases.government_decision_cue: The decision assumes a benign trajectory when the comparable historical reference class shows a non-trivial rate of bad outcomes.

biases.name: Sunk-cost fallacy
biases.definition: Continuing an endeavor because of previously invested resources, rather than marginal future value.
biases.government_decision_cue: Continuation of a program is justified by what has already been spent or committed, rather than by forward-looking cost-benefit analysis.

biases.name: Status quo bias
biases.definition: Preference for the current state of affairs, treating change as a loss.
biases.government_decision_cue: An existing policy is retained without review when its triggering conditions have demonstrably changed, with no stated justification for retention.

biases.name: Endowment effect
biases.definition: People demand more to give up something than they would pay to acquire it.
biases.government_decision_cue: Defense of an existing program, office, or budget line is disproportionate to the case that would be made to create it today.

biases.name: Loss aversion
biases.definition: Losses are psychologically about twice as powerful as equivalent gains.
biases.government_decision_cue: A policy trades a large expected gain for a small reduction in visible downside, with the asymmetry unexplained.

biases.name: Framing effect
biases.definition: Different presentations of the same information produce different decisions.
biases.government_decision_cue: Option presentation in official documents systematically favors one choice (e.g. 'lives saved' vs 'deaths prevented') without counter-framing.

biases.name: Hindsight bias
biases.definition: Tendency to see past events as having been predictable.
biases.government_decision_cue: Post-hoc reviews treat an outcome as having been obvious, scrubbing the uncertainty present at the decision time from the record.

biases.name: Outcome bias
biases.definition: Judging a decision by its outcome rather than by the quality of the decision at the time.
biases.government_decision_cue: A good outcome is cited as vindication of a process that was itself flawed, or a bad outcome triggers sanction of a defensible process.

biases.name: Survivorship bias
biases.definition: Focusing on entities that passed a selection process and overlooking those that did not.
biases.government_decision_cue: A policy is modeled on visible success cases while the larger set of failed comparable cases is unexamined.

biases.name: Selection bias (in evaluation)
biases.definition: Conclusions drawn from a non-representative sample.
biases.government_decision_cue: Program evaluation uses participant data that self-selected, with no correction for the selection effect.

biases.name: Groupthink
biases.definition: Pressure for unanimity in a cohesive group overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives.
biases.government_decision_cue: Meeting minutes show no registered dissent on a complex decision, no devil's-advocate role, and no record of alternatives seriously considered.

biases.name: Authority bias
biases.definition: Tendency to attribute greater accuracy to the opinion of an authority figure.
biases.government_decision_cue: A senior official's assertion overrides contrary technical analysis without the technical analysis being addressed on its merits.

biases.name: In-group bias
biases.definition: Favoring members of one's own group.
biases.government_decision_cue: Contracts, appointments, or exemptions concentrate in a defined affiliation cluster beyond what the qualification pool predicts.

biases.name: Out-group homogeneity effect
biases.definition: Perceiving out-group members as more similar to each other than in-group members are.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy addresses an external population as a monolith, with the heterogeneity of that population not reflected in the design.

biases.name: Halo effect
biases.definition: Overall impression of a person or entity influences judgment of specific traits.
biases.government_decision_cue: Credit given to an institution in one competency is transferred to unrelated competencies without independent evaluation.

biases.name: Horn effect
biases.definition: Negative trait generalizes to unrelated traits.
biases.government_decision_cue: Institution disqualified from one domain is treated as unreliable in unrelated domains without cause.

biases.name: Bandwagon effect
biases.definition: Adoption of a belief because many others hold it.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy alignment across peer jurisdictions is cited as a reason for adoption, with no independent analysis of local fit.

biases.name: False consensus effect
biases.definition: Overestimating the extent to which others share one's views.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy assumes public support that polling or prior consultation does not substantiate.

biases.name: Pluralistic ignorance
biases.definition: Privately held disagreement with a norm while publicly going along, in the mistaken belief one is alone.
biases.government_decision_cue: Internal dissent recorded post-hoc in memoirs or leaks despite unanimous public alignment at decision time.

biases.name: Conformity bias
biases.definition: Alignment of expressed views with group consensus under social pressure.
biases.government_decision_cue: Formal votes or sign-offs show stereotyped unanimity in settings where genuine disagreement would be expected.

biases.name: Just-world hypothesis
biases.definition: Belief that people get what they deserve.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy assumes outcomes reflect merit, treating adverse circumstances as evidence of personal failing without supporting analysis.

biases.name: Fundamental attribution error
biases.definition: Over-attributing others' behavior to disposition, under-attributing to situation.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy design treats a population's behavior as a character trait rather than a response to the constraints the population faces.

biases.name: Actor–observer bias
biases.definition: Attributing own behavior to context and others' to disposition.
biases.government_decision_cue: Institution excuses its own failures with situational reasoning while attributing peer failures to incompetence or bad faith.

biases.name: Self-serving bias
biases.definition: Crediting successes to self, blaming failures on circumstances.
biases.government_decision_cue: After-action reports claim credit for favorable outcomes and attribute unfavorable ones to exogenous shocks.

biases.name: Ultimate attribution error
biases.definition: Group-level extension of attribution biases, favorable to in-group.
biases.government_decision_cue: Coalition partners' errors framed as accidents; opposition errors framed as patterns.

biases.name: Illusion of control
biases.definition: Overestimation of one's ability to control outcomes.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy claims to deliver outcomes that depend substantially on actors, markets, or systems outside the deciding body's reach.

biases.name: Illusion of explanatory depth
biases.definition: People feel they understand complex systems more deeply than they do.
biases.government_decision_cue: Public justification describes a mechanism in slogans; internal technical memoranda show the mechanism was not actually modeled.

biases.name: Illusion of validity
biases.definition: Overestimating the accuracy of one's predictive judgments, especially when information is coherent.
biases.government_decision_cue: Forecasts stated with high confidence despite operating on the kind of input that the relevant reference class handles poorly.

biases.name: Illusion of transparency
biases.definition: Overestimating the degree to which others know one's internal states.
biases.government_decision_cue: Communications assume the public has context the public was never given, and read as evasive for that reason.

biases.name: Spotlight effect
biases.definition: Overestimation of how much one is noticed by others.
biases.government_decision_cue: Decision-makers defend against imagined scrutiny that is not actually present, producing over-elaborate or defensive procedures.

biases.name: Naive realism
biases.definition: Belief that one perceives the world objectively, and that dissenters are biased, uninformed, or irrational.
biases.government_decision_cue: Official framing treats opposition as category-errors rather than as disagreements over facts or values.

biases.name: Hostile attribution bias
biases.definition: Tendency to interpret ambiguous behavior as hostile.
biases.government_decision_cue: Ambiguous acts by counterparties (states, groups) read as adversarial by default, producing escalatory responses.

biases.name: Confabulation (in decision records)
biases.definition: Producing fabricated, distorted, or misinterpreted memories without intent to deceive.
biases.government_decision_cue: Retrospective accounts by the body insert rationales that are not present in the contemporaneous record.

biases.name: Rosy retrospection
biases.definition: Past events recalled more positively than they were judged at the time.
biases.government_decision_cue: Defense of continuing a program relies on a narrative of past success that the contemporaneous evaluation record does not support.

biases.name: Telescoping effect
biases.definition: Misremembering when events occurred.
biases.government_decision_cue: Official narratives compress or stretch timelines in ways that improve the optics, without citing the source of the dates.

biases.name: Peak–end rule
biases.definition: Judging experiences largely by their peak and their end.
biases.government_decision_cue: Program evaluation emphasizes a high point or final event, under-weighting steady-state performance.

biases.name: Recency bias
biases.definition: Over-weighting recent events relative to earlier ones.
biases.government_decision_cue: Trend-based policy leans on the latest data point as if it were a regime change, without testing for reversion.

biases.name: Primacy effect
biases.definition: First items in a sequence better remembered than middle items.
biases.government_decision_cue: Briefings privilege the first option presented; alternatives listed later receive comparatively shallow treatment.

biases.name: Gambler's fallacy
biases.definition: Belief that independent events are affected by prior independent outcomes.
biases.government_decision_cue: Risk planning assumes 'we're due' or 'we've had enough' of a given shock class in a way that treats independent events as dependent.

biases.name: Hot-hand fallacy
biases.definition: Belief that success breeds success in independent trials.
biases.government_decision_cue: A run of favorable outcomes leads to scaling of an intervention without confirming the underlying mechanism.

biases.name: Regression-to-the-mean neglect
biases.definition: Failure to anticipate that extreme observations will moderate.
biases.government_decision_cue: A post-intervention improvement from an extreme baseline is attributed to the intervention without a control or counterfactual.

biases.name: Clustering illusion
biases.definition: Seeing patterns in random data.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy response to a short-run cluster of events treats the cluster as a trend absent significance testing.

biases.name: Conjunction fallacy
biases.definition: Estimating a specific conjunction as more probable than one of its components.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy projections attach probabilities to richly-specified scenarios that exceed the probability of their less-specified parents.

biases.name: Neglect of probability
biases.definition: Disregarding probability information when under uncertainty.
biases.government_decision_cue: Decisions treat low-probability high-salience risks and high-probability low-salience risks as comparable in weight.

biases.name: Zero-risk bias
biases.definition: Preferring to eliminate a small risk completely over reducing a larger risk substantially.
biases.government_decision_cue: Regulation targets full elimination of a minor exposure while leaving a much larger exposure partially addressed.

biases.name: Denominator neglect
biases.definition: Focusing on the numerator of a ratio and neglecting the denominator.
biases.government_decision_cue: Threat communication cites absolute counts of incidents while not reporting the underlying base.

biases.name: Ratio bias
biases.definition: Larger-numerator ratios perceived as higher probability regardless of actual ratio.
biases.government_decision_cue: Communication chooses the numerically larger presentation of a risk (e.g. '10 in 100' vs '1 in 10') to drive perception.

biases.name: Affect heuristic
biases.definition: Using current emotion as a shortcut for risk/benefit judgment.
biases.government_decision_cue: A decision taken during an acute emotional moment departs from the body's standing risk framework without a reasoned update to the framework.

biases.name: Negativity bias
biases.definition: Negative information weighted more than equivalent positive information.
biases.government_decision_cue: Risk-averse response to a single negative signal overrides a weight of positive evidence in the record.

biases.name: Positivity bias
biases.definition: Favorable information weighted more than unfavorable.
biases.government_decision_cue: Press releases and briefings systematically front positive indicators; negative indicators appear only under obligation.

biases.name: Ostrich effect
biases.definition: Avoidance of negative information.
biases.government_decision_cue: Known adverse data is not commissioned, not circulated, or not acted upon at the stage when action was still cheap.

biases.name: Normalcy bias
biases.definition: Underestimating the possibility or severity of a crisis because it has not yet occurred.
biases.government_decision_cue: Warnings from expert bodies are treated as alarmist up until the event, then as obvious after.

biases.name: Dread risk bias
biases.definition: Over-response to vivid low-probability risks relative to equivalently costly diffuse risks.
biases.government_decision_cue: Dramatic incidents prompt resource reallocation far exceeding what equivalent life- or cost-impact diffuse risks receive.

biases.name: Risk compensation
biases.definition: Behavior adjusts to perceived risk level, offsetting protective measures.
biases.government_decision_cue: Expected gains from a safety intervention not realized; behavioral offset not modeled at design time.

biases.name: Observer-expectancy effect
biases.definition: Researcher bias influences subjects or interpretation.
biases.government_decision_cue: Internal studies producing results favorable to the commissioning body disproportionately cited; independent studies downplayed.

biases.name: Experimenter's regress
biases.definition: Difficulty separating what a result is from what it is taken to imply.
biases.government_decision_cue: Studies whose conclusions align with preferred policy treated as settled; equally credentialed studies with opposite conclusions treated as preliminary.

biases.name: Belief bias
biases.definition: Judging the strength of an argument by the believability of its conclusion.
biases.government_decision_cue: Arguments with desired conclusions accepted on lower evidentiary standards than arguments with undesired conclusions.

biases.name: Motivated reasoning
biases.definition: Reasoning shaped by desired conclusions rather than by evidence.
biases.government_decision_cue: Stated rationale follows a conclusion the body had political or personal reason to reach, with the evidentiary chain assembled backward from that conclusion.

biases.name: Identity-protective cognition
biases.definition: Processing information so as to protect one's social identity.
biases.government_decision_cue: Positions on technical questions track factional identity to a degree the underlying technical evidence does not explain.

biases.name: Belief perseverance
biases.definition: Maintaining belief after the evidentiary basis has been discredited.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy maintained after its empirical premise is withdrawn by the originating agency, with no revised rationale substituted.

biases.name: Continued influence effect
biases.definition: Misinformation continues to influence reasoning after retraction.
biases.government_decision_cue: Retracted claims continue to appear in subsequent official talking points, briefings, or justifications.

biases.name: Backfire effect (contested)
biases.definition: Corrections sometimes strengthen the misperception they aim to correct. Effect is contested but documented in some conditions.
biases.government_decision_cue: Official correction is issued in a form that emphasizes the original claim, empirically associated with persistence of the original claim.

biases.name: Escalation of commitment
biases.definition: Increased investment in a course of action in response to its failure.
biases.government_decision_cue: Failing program receives additional resources under the same theory of action, with no independent re-examination of the theory.

biases.name: Narrative fallacy
biases.definition: Imposing a coherent story on historical data where one is not warranted.
biases.government_decision_cue: Official history of a policy area is told as a causally connected sequence, with the contingency and noise in the actual record edited out.

biases.name: Texas sharpshooter fallacy
biases.definition: Drawing the target around the clustered hits after the fact.
biases.government_decision_cue: Success criteria for an initiative announced or revised after outcomes are known.

biases.name: Goodhart's law as bias
biases.definition: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
biases.government_decision_cue: Performance metrics attached to incentives produce gaming at the reporting layer, with no independent verification of the underlying state.

biases.name: Streetlight effect
biases.definition: Searching where it is easy, not where the answer is.
biases.government_decision_cue: Investigations or reviews focus on easily-accessible records while the decisive records remain uncollected.

biases.name: Parkinson's law of triviality
biases.definition: Disproportionate deliberation on trivial items because they are understandable.
biases.government_decision_cue: Meeting records show long debate on minor line items and pro-forma sign-off on larger consequential ones.

biases.name: Zero-sum bias
biases.definition: Tendency to view mixed-motive interactions as pure win/lose.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy defaults to positional bargaining in situations where integrative options are documented in the record and declined without analysis.

biases.name: Reactive devaluation
biases.definition: Proposals devalued because of who proposes them.
biases.government_decision_cue: Same proposal accepted from one source and rejected from another, with no substantive difference in the content.

biases.name: Not-invented-here syndrome
biases.definition: Resistance to ideas originating outside the group.
biases.government_decision_cue: External best-practice adopted belatedly or rebranded; internal inferior alternative preferred meanwhile.

biases.name: Proportionality bias
biases.definition: Big outcomes must have big causes.
biases.government_decision_cue: Response to a large event dismisses mundane-but-adequate causal explanations in favor of conspiratorial or outsized framings.

biases.name: Hyperbolic discounting
biases.definition: Stronger preference for smaller-sooner over larger-later rewards.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy preference for near-term visible wins over larger deferred gains, with no stated discount-rate rationale.

biases.name: Present bias
biases.definition: Discounting future costs and benefits relative to present ones.
biases.government_decision_cue: Fiscal decisions defer costs past the current administration's horizon in structurally predictable patterns.

biases.name: Projection bias
biases.definition: Assuming future preferences will match current ones.
biases.government_decision_cue: Long-range plans assume current public opinion is stable across the plan's horizon, without sensitivity analysis.

biases.name: Focalism (focusing illusion)
biases.definition: Overweighting a single salient factor.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy debate fixates on a single metric to the exclusion of the broader objective function the policy is meant to serve.

biases.name: Impact bias
biases.definition: Overestimating the emotional impact of future events.
biases.government_decision_cue: Decision-makers expect catastrophic public reaction to an option and reject it; the comparable historical reference class does not support the expectation.

biases.name: Empathy gap (hot/cold)
biases.definition: Underestimating how future affective states will shift one's preferences.
biases.government_decision_cue: Contingency plans drafted in calm conditions assume calm execution; crisis responses deviate from the plan predictably under stress.

biases.name: Moral licensing
biases.definition: Past good behavior licenses later problematic behavior.
biases.government_decision_cue: Prior rights-protecting action cited as license for later rights-curtailing action in an unrelated domain.

biases.name: Moral credentialing
biases.definition: Claimed moral standing used to dismiss scrutiny.
biases.government_decision_cue: Appeals to the body's past record used in place of a substantive answer to a specific current question.

biases.name: System justification
biases.definition: Defense of existing arrangements even when they disadvantage oneself or one's group.
biases.government_decision_cue: Institutional arrangements defended with reasoning that does not engage with the critique on its merits.

biases.name: Backfire through reactance
biases.definition: Pressure produces opposite compliance.
biases.government_decision_cue: Mandates produce measurable counter-compliance predicted in the pre-decision record but not mitigated in design.

biases.name: Naive cynicism
biases.definition: Expecting more egocentric bias in others than in oneself.
biases.government_decision_cue: Opposing parties' positions explained by self-interest; own side's by principle, with no symmetry check.

biases.name: Illusory superiority
biases.definition: Overestimating one's qualities relative to others.
biases.government_decision_cue: Self-assessment of institutional performance materially exceeds independent benchmarks.

biases.name: Hard–easy effect
biases.definition: Overconfidence on hard tasks; underconfidence on easy tasks.
biases.government_decision_cue: Confidence in complex forecasts exceeds confidence in simple ones, inverting the calibrated pattern.

biases.name: Bias blind spot
biases.definition: Seeing bias in others more readily than in oneself.
biases.government_decision_cue: Post-mortem attributes errors to external actors' biases without examining the same biases in the deciding body.

biases.name: Third-person effect
biases.definition: Perceiving mass-media messages as affecting others more than oneself.
biases.government_decision_cue: Officials regulate a media or information channel on the theory that others will be misled by it, while drawing on the same channel themselves.

biases.name: Illusory truth effect
biases.definition: Repetition increases perceived truthfulness.
biases.government_decision_cue: Un-evidenced claim becomes treated as baseline through repetition in official communication, without an intervening substantiation step.

biases.name: Familiarity principle (mere exposure)
biases.definition: Preference for things because they are familiar.
biases.government_decision_cue: Incumbent vendors, consultants, or frameworks retained through familiarity in the face of documented deficits.

biases.name: Cheerleader effect
biases.definition: Individuals appear more attractive in a group.
biases.government_decision_cue: A weaker proposal bundled with stronger proposals clears review on the bundle's merits without item-level scrutiny.

biases.name: Pseudocertainty effect
biases.definition: Certainty in part of a multi-stage outcome produces risk-averse choice.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy locks in a risk-averse step on a conditional outcome that is itself uncertain, inflating apparent certainty.

biases.name: Certainty effect
biases.definition: Outcomes perceived as certain over-weighted versus merely probable.
biases.government_decision_cue: A guarantee framing commands a disproportionate premium over a statistically superior probabilistic alternative.

biases.name: Isolation effect (Kahneman–Tversky)
biases.definition: Stripping common components from choices changes the choice.
biases.government_decision_cue: Choices presented with and without their shared context produce inconsistent official preferences within the same decision window.

biases.name: Magnitude insensitivity
biases.definition: Willingness to pay for an outcome does not scale with the outcome's size.
biases.government_decision_cue: Budgets attached to small and large versions of the same problem are roughly comparable, out of proportion to the problem's scale.

biases.name: Scope insensitivity
biases.definition: Evaluations of public goods do not scale with scope.
biases.government_decision_cue: Contingent-valuation-style justifications cite comparable willingness figures for very different-scale programs.

biases.name: Mental accounting
biases.definition: Treating money differently depending on its source or designation.
biases.government_decision_cue: Funds in different ledgers treated as non-fungible when the legal record permits fungibility, with efficiency costs.

biases.name: Compromise effect
biases.definition: Preference for middle options in a set.
biases.government_decision_cue: Three-option framings in official reviews systematically converge on the middle option regardless of the underlying merit distribution.

biases.name: Decoy effect
biases.definition: Addition of an asymmetrically dominated option shifts choice toward the dominating one.
biases.government_decision_cue: A third option introduced into a review appears present to shift preference between the other two, not as a serious candidate.

biases.name: Less-is-better effect
biases.definition: Smaller set preferred in isolation, larger set preferred jointly.
biases.government_decision_cue: Public messaging prefers smaller numerical claims presented alone to larger claims presented with context.

biases.name: Unit bias
biases.definition: Default portion or grain treated as the correct amount.
biases.government_decision_cue: Program sizing defaults to round administrative units rather than analytically derived thresholds.

biases.name: Default effect
biases.definition: The pre-selected option has disproportionate uptake.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy design sets a default that materially changes outcomes, presented as neutral.

biases.name: Choice overload
biases.definition: Too many options reduce choice quality and satisfaction.
biases.government_decision_cue: Consultation processes present so many options that structured ranking is impossible and the body selects by default.

biases.name: Attentional bias
biases.definition: Ongoing thoughts influence perception.
biases.government_decision_cue: A salient ongoing concern leads to systematic over-detection of that concern's signatures in incoming reports.

biases.name: Attribute substitution
biases.definition: Answering a hard question by answering an easier one without noticing.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy analysis answers 'is this popular' when the brief called for 'does this work'.

biases.name: WYSIATI (what you see is all there is)
biases.definition: Treating available information as sufficient.
biases.government_decision_cue: Decisions conclude from the data at hand without commissioning or requesting the data that is absent but obtainable.

biases.name: Illusory correlation
biases.definition: Seeing relationships between variables where none exist.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy rationale asserts a causal link between variables that co-vary in noisy data but not in controlled analysis.

biases.name: Prevalence-induced concept change
biases.definition: As a phenomenon becomes less common, the concept expands to keep prevalence constant.
biases.government_decision_cue: The definition of a harm or threat expands over time in the body's own materials in a way that keeps reported incidence stable.

biases.name: Denomination effect
biases.definition: Larger denominations spent less readily than the equivalent in smaller ones.
biases.government_decision_cue: Consolidated block grants committed more conservatively than the same sum split across many line items.

biases.name: Pro-innovation bias
biases.definition: Overestimation of an innovation's usefulness and underestimation of its costs.
biases.government_decision_cue: Emerging-technology procurement cites benefits with precision and costs with hand-waving.

biases.name: Pessimism bias
biases.definition: Overestimating the probability of negative outcomes.
biases.government_decision_cue: Threat estimates systematically exceed historical base rates without stated revision of the base rate.

biases.name: Illusion of asymmetric insight
biases.definition: Belief that one understands others better than others understand oneself.
biases.government_decision_cue: Official framings claim to know the opposition's true motives while asserting the opposition misunderstands one's own.

biases.name: False uniqueness effect
biases.definition: Overestimating the uniqueness of one's own abilities.
biases.government_decision_cue: Institutional self-narrative positions the body as uniquely equipped in a role where peer benchmarks show comparable capacity elsewhere.

biases.name: Worse-than-average effect
biases.definition: For difficult tasks, self-ratings below average.
biases.government_decision_cue: On hard technical items the body under-claims capacity it in fact has, declining to act.

biases.name: Confabulated unanimity
biases.definition: Groups remember themselves as more unanimous than they were.
biases.government_decision_cue: Retrospective accounts of a deliberation claim unanimity that the contemporaneous minutes or votes do not support.

biases.name: Risky shift / group polarization
biases.definition: Group decisions move to the extremes of pre-discussion tendencies.
biases.government_decision_cue: Committee outputs more extreme than the median pre-meeting position of members.

biases.name: Shared-information bias
biases.definition: Groups spend more time on information members already share.
biases.government_decision_cue: Minutes show discussion time dominated by consensus points, with unshared specialist knowledge from individual members surfacing only briefly or not at all.

biases.name: Abilene paradox
biases.definition: Groups pursue a course no individual member privately favors, each misreading the others.
biases.government_decision_cue: A decision no senior figure later defends as their own preference was nevertheless approved unanimously.

biases.name: Diffusion of responsibility
biases.definition: Responsibility diffuses across a group, reducing individual action.
biases.government_decision_cue: A duty-to-act visible to multiple bodies goes undischarged with each citing another's jurisdiction.

biases.name: Free-rider effect
biases.definition: Members rely on others' contribution to a shared task.
biases.government_decision_cue: Coalition commitments met by a subset while others under-contribute relative to stated share.

biases.name: Social loafing
biases.definition: Reduced individual effort in group contexts.
biases.government_decision_cue: Interagency bodies produce less per-member output than comparable single-agency work-streams.

biases.name: Social proof
biases.definition: Behavior copied from others as evidence of correctness.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy adopted primarily because a peer jurisdiction adopted it, with local-fit analysis absent or cursory.

biases.name: Commitment and consistency bias
biases.definition: Drive to act consistently with prior public commitments.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy held in place past the point its empirical premise supports, because reversal would be visibly inconsistent.

biases.name: Reciprocity bias (in regulatory capture context)
biases.definition: Tendency to return favors, exploited in policy settings.
biases.government_decision_cue: Pattern of decisions favorable to a regulated entity correlates with prior benefits flowing from that entity, above what policy merits alone would predict.

biases.name: Liking bias
biases.definition: Preference toward those we like.
biases.government_decision_cue: Selection decisions correlate with relational or affinity signals orthogonal to merit criteria.

biases.name: Scarcity bias
biases.definition: Over-valuation of what is scarce.
biases.government_decision_cue: Artificially scarce policy slots (permits, licenses) produce evaluation shortcuts favoring early or well-placed applicants.

biases.name: Contrast effect
biases.definition: Judgment of an item depends on what it is compared to.
biases.government_decision_cue: A policy is rated favorably against a straw-alternative when the defensible comparison would include a stronger peer.

biases.name: Distinction bias
biases.definition: Options compared side-by-side appear more different than when evaluated separately.
biases.government_decision_cue: Side-by-side review produces ranking decisions that diverge from separate-evaluation results, without the divergence being noted.

biases.name: Illusion of clarity
biases.definition: Own communications feel clearer to the speaker than to the audience.
biases.government_decision_cue: Official communication tested post-hoc reveals audience comprehension far below the drafters' expectation; no pre-release testing was conducted.

biases.name: Curse of knowledge
biases.definition: Experts fail to model what non-experts do not know.
biases.government_decision_cue: Public-facing materials assume technical fluency the population does not have, reducing effective access to the program.

biases.name: Egocentric bias
biases.definition: Over-reliance on one's own perspective.
biases.government_decision_cue: Consultation processes weight input from constituencies closest to the deciding body's own demographics.

biases.name: Naive empiricism
biases.definition: Over-trust in selected empirical evidence absent a considered methodology.
biases.government_decision_cue: Cherry-picked datasets cited as decisive without accounting for the excluded data in the same record.

biases.name: Law of the instrument
biases.definition: Over-reliance on a familiar tool.
biases.government_decision_cue: A well-known policy instrument applied to a problem where evaluation shows the instrument is poorly matched.

biases.name: Semmelweis reflex
biases.definition: Reflexive rejection of new evidence that contradicts established paradigms.
biases.government_decision_cue: New methodological findings from internal or external bodies sidelined with procedural rather than substantive objections.

biases.name: Pro-forma compliance
biases.definition: Compliance through procedure without attention to substance.
biases.government_decision_cue: Risk assessments and consultations conducted in the prescribed form but with no evidence the output affected the decision.

biases.name: Motivated skepticism
biases.definition: Skepticism selectively applied to undesired conclusions.
biases.government_decision_cue: Methodological standards raised specifically for studies with inconvenient findings; convenient findings accepted at a lower bar.

biases.name: Illusion of agency
biases.definition: Overestimating one's causal role in outcomes.
biases.government_decision_cue: Outcomes arising predominantly from exogenous factors attributed to policy action in official communications.

biases.name: Illusion of moral superiority
biases.definition: Self-rated ethics systematically above average.
biases.government_decision_cue: Institutional self-description systematically surpasses independent ethics reviews.

biases.name: Moral luck neglect
biases.definition: Ignoring the role of luck in moral and performance assessments.
biases.government_decision_cue: Credit and blame assigned without isolating the component of the outcome the deciding body could have controlled.

biases.name: Single-cause fallacy
biases.definition: Treating multi-causal outcomes as having one cause.
biases.government_decision_cue: Official explanations for complex failures or successes name a single cause, suppressing documented co-causes.

biases.name: Monocausal framing under uncertainty
biases.definition: Forcing single-cause narratives under irreducible multi-causal uncertainty.
biases.government_decision_cue: Preliminary investigations publicly name a cause before the evidentiary phase permits single-cause conclusions.

biases.name: Regression neglect in program evaluation
biases.definition: Mistaking mean reversion for program effect.
biases.government_decision_cue: Programs targeted at extreme baseline conditions evaluated without controls; improvement claimed as attributable.

biases.name: Publication / reporting asymmetry
biases.definition: Selective release of favorable results.
biases.government_decision_cue: Commissioning body releases favorable internal studies and withholds or delays unfavorable ones.

biases.name: Halo-contamination in appointments
biases.definition: Appointment decisions driven by reputation in unrelated domains.
biases.government_decision_cue: Appointee's high-profile unrelated success cited in lieu of domain-specific qualification in the appointment record.

biases.name: Normality creep
biases.definition: Gradual normalization of previously-unacceptable conduct.
biases.government_decision_cue: Procedural thresholds relaxed step-wise over time, with no step alone large enough to trigger review, cumulative change material.

biases.name: Base-rate substitution by anecdote
biases.definition: A single vivid case displaces the statistical base rate in deliberation.
biases.government_decision_cue: Testimony from one case drives a policy whose operating parameters affect a population whose base rate does not match the testimony.

biases.name: Evidence discounting by source friction
biases.definition: Evidence is discounted by how inconvenient it is to act on.
biases.government_decision_cue: Findings requiring costly action face higher evidentiary scrutiny than findings supporting the status quo.

biases.name: Pre-commitment lock-in
biases.definition: Prior public commitments reduce willingness to update.
biases.government_decision_cue: Campaign- or coalition-level commitments cited as reason to maintain policies inconsistent with updated evidence.

biases.name: Risk homeostasis
biases.definition: Populations maintain target risk levels; safety gains offset by behavior.
biases.government_decision_cue: Safety interventions model the direct effect only; the risk-substitution effect is absent from the impact assessment.

biases.name: Theory-induced blindness
biases.definition: A dominant theory makes anomalies invisible.
biases.government_decision_cue: Persistent anomalies in program data are reclassified rather than treated as anomalies; the underlying theory is not revisited.

biases.name: Substitution of intention for action
biases.definition: Announced intent treated as if it were the action.
biases.government_decision_cue: Press releases announce an action; the administrative record shows the action was not commenced or funded.

biases.name: Present-bias in enforcement
biases.definition: Enforcement intensity declines with distance from the originating event.
biases.government_decision_cue: Violation-response data show sharp enforcement immediately post-incident, decaying rapidly independent of continuing violation.

biases.name: Consistency-preservation over truth
biases.definition: Updating language rather than position to preserve apparent consistency.
biases.government_decision_cue: Official position on a question is described as unchanged while the operative definition of the question has shifted.

biases.name: Expert deference overshoot
biases.definition: Over-deference to experts outside their domain of expertise.
biases.government_decision_cue: An expert's authority in one technical area is extended to cover normative or cross-domain questions their expertise does not address.

biases.name: Expert deference undershoot
biases.definition: Under-use of relevant expertise in favor of lay intuition.
biases.government_decision_cue: Technical decisions with established expert consensus decided against the consensus without a specific technical rebuttal.

biases.name: Forecast anchoring to prior forecast
biases.definition: New forecasts anchored to prior public forecasts rather than to underlying data.
biases.government_decision_cue: Successive official forecasts show suspicious stability relative to the volatility of the underlying series.

biases.name: Consensus display without consensus
biases.definition: Visible consensus produced by process design rather than agreement.
biases.government_decision_cue: Joint communiqués show agreement on items that internal documents show as contested.

biases.name: Salience-driven agenda setting
biases.definition: The agenda follows salience rather than severity.
biases.government_decision_cue: Time and budget allocations track media salience of issues rather than independent severity signals.

biases.name: Elite-sample generalization
biases.definition: Drawing population conclusions from elite samples.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policies designed on the basis of consultations with non-representative elite stakeholders project their preferences onto the population.

biases.name: Representativeness-by-case in legal drafting
biases.definition: Drafting law around a vivid case, ignoring the case's representativeness.
biases.government_decision_cue: Statute drafted in response to a specific incident is structurally misfit for the population of cases it will now govern.

biases.name: Over-fitting to anecdote in enforcement
biases.definition: Enforcement practice overfits to the case that triggered it.
biases.government_decision_cue: Enforcement guidance tracks the features of the triggering case to a degree that produces selective application.

biases.name: Temporal discounting of diffuse victims
biases.definition: Diffuse future victims under-weighted vs. identified present beneficiaries.
biases.government_decision_cue: Cost-benefit analyses weight identifiable current beneficiaries fully and future statistical beneficiaries at systematically reduced weight.

biases.name: Identifiable victim effect
biases.definition: Greater willingness to help an identified individual than an equivalent statistical life.
biases.government_decision_cue: Resource allocation responds to named cases while equivalent diffuse need receives less, beyond what published prioritization rules predict.

biases.name: Precedent inertia
biases.definition: Over-weighting prior decisions as justification.
biases.government_decision_cue: Precedent cited as controlling where precedent's factual basis does not apply; no distinguishing analysis performed.

biases.name: Availability cascades
biases.definition: Self-reinforcing belief formation through media and social amplification.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy activated by a rapidly amplifying public discourse where the underlying incidence has not changed materially.

biases.name: Moral outrage overshoot in regulation
biases.definition: Regulatory severity calibrated to public emotion rather than to harm.
biases.government_decision_cue: Penalty structures in newly-enacted rules exceed the scaling implied by the harm function in the accompanying impact assessment.

biases.name: Risk transfer illusion
biases.definition: Transferring risk perceived as eliminating it.
biases.government_decision_cue: Policy reassigns risk to another party (insurer, private operator, subnational unit) and treats the transfer as risk reduction in the headline framing.

biases.name: Procedural laundering
biases.definition: Legitimacy sought through process checklists rather than outcomes.
biases.government_decision_cue: Criticism on substance is answered by pointing to process compliance, without substantive rebuttal.

biases.name: Information-cascade in committees
biases.definition: Later speakers update on earlier speakers' signals, producing herding.
biases.government_decision_cue: Early strong signals by senior speakers correlate with sharp convergence of subsequent statements in the same meeting.

biases.name: Illusory progress
biases.definition: Activity metrics mistaken for outcome progress.
biases.government_decision_cue: Progress reports dominated by input/activity metrics (meetings held, consultations opened) absent an outcome benchmark.

biases.name: Scapegoating in review
biases.definition: Attribution of system failure to an individual.
biases.government_decision_cue: Post-incident review concludes with a single individual's fault while the system conditions that produced the failure remain unchanged.

biases.name: Sanctity-of-mission inertia
biases.definition: Mission statement used to resist even evidence-driven scope revision.
biases.government_decision_cue: Mandate revision rejected on identity grounds rather than on evidence or cost grounds.

biases.name: Complexity-avoidance simplification
biases.definition: Policy simplified to a legible form that the underlying problem does not support.
biases.government_decision_cue: Decision rests on a simplification whose failure modes are described in the underlying analysis but not reflected in the policy.

biases.name: Combined-function conflict absorption
biases.definition: A single body holding two mandates whose evidentiary intake structure favors one mandate over the other absorbs contrary signals asymmetrically, without the asymmetry being represented in its self-description.
biases.government_decision_cue: An agency with both a revenue/commercial mandate and a safety/regulatory mandate over the same industry accepts operator representations at a lower evidentiary bar than it applies to independent technical signals, while describing its regime as even-handed.

biases.name: Source monoculture
biases.definition: The briefings, advisors, intelligence streams, or expert panels feeding a decision draw from a homogeneous origin (single agency, single ideological cluster, single contractor, single vetted list), and the homogeneity is not justified by the question being decided.
biases.government_decision_cue: Briefing logs, advisor rosters, or witness lists for the deliberation show one channel or one network supplying the bulk of inputs; alternative sources of comparable standing existed but were not engaged, with no documented reason for their exclusion.

biases.name: Structural dissent suppression
biases.definition: Dissenting analyses existed within the body's reach (internal memos, alternative-views channels, minority reports, dissenting expert testimony) and were not surfaced in the deliberation record, were demoted, classified out of view, or routed past the deciders. The suppression is a property of the routing system, not of any one decider's hostility to the dissent.
biases.government_decision_cue: A dissenting memo, footnote, minority report, or alt-views annex is later shown to have existed at decision time but was absent from the briefing pack, marked at a classification the deciders did not hold, or annexed in a position the briefing pack did not surface.

biases.name: Briefing-pipeline closure
biases.definition: The intermediate stages between primary source and decider compress, summarize, or prioritize inputs in ways that eliminate uncertainty bands, dissent, or counter-evidence before they reach the room. The deciders see a cleaner record than exists.
biases.government_decision_cue: Comparison of the source stratum (raw analyses, working-level memos) with the decision-level briefing shows systematic loss of caveats, ranges, or contrary findings; the briefing pack is more confident than its underlying inputs warrant.

biases.name: Selection-for-agreement in personnel
biases.definition: Personnel changes preceding the decision systematically replace dissenting voices with concurring ones, with the dissenting voices' published positions documented in the prior record. The deliberation that follows is structurally unable to surface the prior dissent.
biases.government_decision_cue: Departures, reassignments, non-renewals, or appointments in the months before the decision shift the balance of the deliberating body in one direction; the displaced individuals had documented prior positions on the question that the new composition does not represent.

biases.name: Closed-loop validation
biases.definition: The body's outbound communications are addressed primarily to audiences whose composition mirrors its own inputs (friendly press, allied agencies, in-network experts), so that incoming feedback re-confirms the original frame. There is no scheduled exposure to hostile-witness, red-team, or adversarial-review channels.
biases.government_decision_cue: Press, consultation, and review channels used after the decision overlap heavily with the channels used before it; no adversarial review (independent audit, opposition-staffed panel, formal devil's advocate) is scheduled into the process.

biases.name: Adversarial-channel atrophy
biases.definition: Standing channels designed to deliver contradiction (inspectors general, statutory minority counsel, alt-analysis cells, ombuds, scientific advisory boards with dissent rights) exist on paper but are under-resourced, vacant, bypassed, or have had their reporting lines shortened so that their findings do not reach the deliberation.
biases.government_decision_cue: An adversarial channel that the body's own framework assumes (e.g. an alt-analysis cell, an IG, a statutory advisory board) is unstaffed, last reported years ago, has its reports buried at a depth the deciders do not read to, or had its access revoked before the decision.

biases.name: Sequential sign-off without convergent debate
biases.definition: A decision is built by passing a draft from station to station for individual sign-off, never assembling the signers in one room to compare reasoning. Each signer assumes the others have done the substantive work; no one has.
biases.government_decision_cue: The decision artifact carries a chain of initials or stamps but no record of a convening, no minutes of a debate, and no document showing the signers' reasoning was compared; the chain is the only deliberation evidence.

biases.name: Dissent-cost asymmetry
biases.definition: The structural cost of registering dissent inside the body (career risk, exclusion from future briefings, reputational exposure to the chair) is materially higher than the cost of concurring, and the chair tolerates the asymmetry. Silence ceases to be evidence of agreement.
biases.government_decision_cue: The body's prior record shows dissenters were demoted, transferred, excluded from subsequent meetings, or publicly criticized by the chair; the cost is documented and was not corrected; subsequent meetings show progressively narrower expressed disagreement.
